chain.g: to take, lay hold of, grasp, strike

ety.text: From Middle English taken (“to take, lay hold of, grasp, strike”), from Old English tacan (“to grasp, touch”), probably of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse taka (“to touch, take”). Alternatively, inherited from Proto-West Germanic *takan (“to take; grasp, touch”). Both from Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to touch”), from pre-Germanic *deh₁g- (“to touch”), possibly a phonetically altered form of Proto-Indo-European *te-th₂g- (“to touch, take”) (see there for details). Gradually displaced native English nim, from Middle English nimen, from Old English niman (“to take”).

senses.d: To get into one's hands, possession, or control, with or without force.
ex: They took Charlton's gun from his cold, dead hands.
I'll take that plate off the table.

senses.d: To seize or capture.
ex: take the guards prisoner
take prisoners

senses.d: To catch or get possession of (fish or game).
ex: took ten catfish in one afternoon

senses.d: To catch the ball; especially as a wicket-keeper and after the batsman has missed or edged it.
To appropriate or transfer into one's own possession, sometimes by physically carrying off.
ex: Billy took her pencil.
The County took his land by eminent domain.

senses.d: To exact.
ex: take a toll
take revenge

senses.d: To capture or win (a piece or trick) in a game.
ex: took the next two tricks
took Smith's rook

senses.d: To receive or accept (something, especially something which was given).
ex: took third place
took bribes

senses.d: To receive or accept (something) as payment or compensation.
ex: The store doesn't take checks.
She wouldn't take any money for her help.

senses.d: To accept and follow (advice, etc.).
ex: take my advice

senses.d: An act of taking.
ex: 'I saw you in Norfolk doing twenty-odd takes with that fisherman chap and it looked perfect in the rushes.'

senses.d: Money that is taken in, (legal or illegal) proceeds, income; (in particular) profits; takings.
ex: He wants half of the take if he helps with the job.
The mayor is on the take.

senses.d: The or a quantity of fish, game animals or pelts, etc which have been taken at one time; catch.
ex: Since a state ban was lifted in 1984, hunters may shoot one swan per season. A permit system limited last season's take to 6,000.

senses.d: An interpretation or view, opinion or assessment; perspective; a statement expressing such a position.
ex: What's your take on this issue, Fred?
Another unsolicited maths take: talking about quotients in terms of "equivalence classes" or cosets is really unnatural.

senses.d: An approach, a (distinct) treatment.
ex: a new take on a traditional dish
Whatever the provenance, the result is a delightfully novel take on a stalwart, often deadening Victorian feature.

senses.d: A scene recorded (filmed) at one time, without an interruption or break; a recording of such a scene.
ex: It's a take.
Act seven, scene three, take two.

senses.d: A recording of a musical performance made during an uninterrupted single recording period.
A visible (facial) response to something, especially something unexpected; a facial gesture in response to an event.
ex: did a double take and then a triple take
I did a take when I saw the new car in the driveway.

senses.d: An instance of successful inoculation/vaccination.
A catch of the ball (in cricket, especially one by the wicket-keeper).

Eventually /ʎ-/ spread to the entire verb paradigm by analogy.

From Middle English taken, takenn, from Old English tacen, *ġetacen, from Old Norse tekinn, from Proto-Germanic *tēkanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to take; grasp; touch”). Cognate with Scots takin, tane, Danish tagen, Swedish tagen, Icelandic tekin. Morphologically take + -n.

senses.d: Infatuated; fond of or attracted to.
ex: He was very taken with the girl, I hear.

senses.d: In a serious romantic relationship.
ex: I can't ask her out, she's taken.

senses.d: Alluring; attractive.
ex: His speech from the hustings was very original, and therefore very taking.

senses.d: Infectious; contagious.
ex:
All the stor’d vengeances of heaven fall
On her ingrateful top! Strike her young bones,
You taking airs, with lameness!

Come not near me,
For I am yet too taking for your company.

senses.d: The act by which something is taken.
ex: At the taking of the stockade he had distinguished himself greatly by the methodical ferocity of his fighting.

senses.d: A seizure of someone's goods or possessions.
A state of mental distress, resulting in excited or erratic behavior (in the expression in a taking).
ex: What a taking was hee in, when your husband askt who was in the basket?
‘Poor soul - she was quite in a taking. You see, she’d opened the door to the next compartment by mistake.’

senses.d: Cash or money received (by a shop or other business, for example).
ex: Fred was concerned because the takings from his sweetshop had fallen again for the third week.
Count the shop's takings.

grp.label: act by which something is taken

ety.text: Deverbal from tomar (“to take”).
From tomar + -dura.
Deverbal from take over.

senses.d: The purchase of one company by another; a merger without the formation of a new company, especially where some stakeholders in the purchased company oppose the purchase.
The acquisition of a public company whose shares are listed on a stock exchange, in contrast to the acquisition of a private company.
A time or event in which control or authority, especially over a facility is passed from one party to the next.
ex: Revollo was absent when Bolivian police and the navy captain arrived at dawn, and the base takeover came off without problems, according to a U.S. narcotics official.

senses.d: An event at which teens gather in public and act out; a street takeover.
